The repair shop opened at nine, though its owner, Mara, usually arrived earlier. She liked the hour before customers came, when the street was quiet enough for her to hear the radiator clicking and the pigeons shifting on the windowsill. She would unlock the door, set a kettle on the stove, and examine whatever had been left on her workbench the night before. A lamp with a broken switch. A radio that only whispered. A wooden toy missing one wheel. Most mornings, she had no idea whether she could fix any of them. That uncertainty was part of the pleasure.

The shop had once belonged to her father, who repaired watches and clocks. He had been a patient man with enormous hands, and as a child Mara had found it miraculous that his fingers could handle screws smaller than grains of rice. He taught her to lay each component on a clean cloth, in the order it had been removed. “Memory is useful,” he said, “but it shouldn’t have to do all the work.” After he died, Mara kept the shop, though she expanded its purpose. She repaired almost anything she could lift onto the bench, and sometimes things she couldn’t.

One wet Tuesday, a boy brought her a small blue suitcase. He set it on the counter with both hands, as if it contained something breakable. Its handle had come loose on one side, and a strip of silver tape clung to the corner. Mara asked what was inside. “Nothing now,” the boy said. “It’s for my mother.” He explained that she was going away for a few weeks to take care of his grandmother. The suitcase had been hers when she was young, and she preferred it to the larger one in the hall. She said it was easier to carry on the train.

Mara tested the handle. The leather had split around an old rivet, but the rest of it was sound. She told the boy she could replace the rivet and reinforce the leather, though the repair would be visible. He considered this with the seriousness of a customer ordering furniture. “Will it look bad?” he asked. Mara opened a drawer and took out a piece of leather almost the same shade as the handle. “Different,” she said. “Probably not bad.” The boy nodded, then asked how much it would cost. When she told him, he counted coins onto the counter, arranging them into small towers.

While she worked, he sat on a stool near the window. His name was Leo, he told her, and his mother had tried to mend the handle herself. The tape had held for one trip to the market and then given way as she came through the front door. He had picked the suitcase up for her, but by then she was laughing, with groceries spread across the floor. Mara could see where they had cleaned a little milk from the blue lining. Leo watched as she fitted the new leather beneath the old and pressed a brass rivet into place.

When the suitcase was ready, he lifted it carefully and gave the handle a cautious tug. Then he swung it once, just above the floor. Mara was about to warn him not to hit the counter, but he stopped in time. He thanked her and carried it out into the rain, holding it under his coat. Through the window, she watched him pause at the corner to make sure it was covered. The coat was not quite wide enough, and one blue edge showed beneath it. He adjusted his grip and set off again, walking quickly toward the bus stop.

The following morning, Mara found an envelope beneath the door. Inside was a photograph of a woman standing beside a much younger version of herself, both holding the blue suitcase. It took Mara a moment to understand: the picture showed Leo’s mother with his grandmother, years earlier, outside a railway station. On the back, someone had written, “Thank you. It’s still going.” Mara placed the photograph on a shelf behind the counter. Customers sometimes noticed it and asked who the people were. She told them what she knew, which was only a little, and then usually returned to the object they had brought in.

As winter approached, the shop grew busier. People came with heaters that rattled and kettles that no longer switched off. A woman brought in a music box that had belonged to her brother, asking whether Mara could make it play again before his birthday. The tune was slow and uncertain when Mara first turned the key, but a cleaning and a small adjustment helped. When the woman collected it, she listened all the way through, holding the open box near her face. Then she closed it, paid, and asked whether Mara could also look at a toaster the next week.

Not every job ended so well. Some parts were impossible to find, and some objects had been damaged beyond what Mara knew how to mend. She kept a notebook of these failures, partly so she could recognize the same problem if it appeared again. In its pages were sketches of cracked gears, names of manufacturers, and questions she meant to ask other repairers. Occasionally she turned back to an old entry and found an answer she hadn’t had before. More often, the notes remained unresolved. She kept them anyway; they helped her explain to customers what she had tried.

Years later, Leo returned to the shop carrying a radio. He was taller, and Mara did not recognize him until he pointed to the photograph on the shelf. His grandmother had died that spring, he said. His mother had brought the radio home from her house, and they had found the blue suitcase in a cupboard there too. It was scuffed now, but the handle was still attached. Mara turned the radio over and removed its back panel. Leo leaned across the counter to watch, and she handed him the screws, one by one, to lay on a clean cloth.
